newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany celebrates Jewish leader's 70th birthday.
newsitem.headline: Germany celebrates Jewish leader's 70th birthday.

text.p: Germany's Jewish leader Ignatz Bubis, celebrating his 70th birthday on Sunday with top German political leaders, said there was still tension between Jews and non-Jews more than 50 years after the end of the Holocaust.

German President Roman Herzog hosted a banquet in Bubis' honour for 100 guests including Jewish leaders from across the world, and political and religious leaders from Germany on Sunday evening at his Berlin presidential palace.
"We still don't have a normal relationship...between Jews and non-Jews in Germany," Bubis told Reuters Television on Saturday.
"Many non-Jewish Germans still see Jews as foreigners."
Bubis, a Holocaust survivor who has sometimes been criticised for making things "too easy" for the Germans, said his main task now was to try to ease these tensions further.

Tributes poured in at the weekend from political leaders and the media for the man, who for many Germans has become a household name and figure of moral authority since he became the leader of Germany's 50,000-strong Jewish community in 1992.

Herzog, who described the occasion as a "state ceremony disguised as a birthday party", paid tribute to Bubis for his efforts to help revive Germany's Jewish community and normalise relations between Jews and non-Jews.

"In the name of Germany I thank you for what you have done for the welfare and standing of our country," Herzog said, praising Bubis for visiting 300,000 pupils in German schools to relate his personal experience of the Holocaust as a Jew.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl plans to travel to Bubis' office in Frankfurt on Monday morning to congratulate him in person and join in more birthday celebrations. Kohl praised him for acting as a unifying force in German society.
"Your credibility, your readiness for reconciliation and tolerance have won you respect and recognition in all sections of society," Kohl told Bubis in a personal birthday message.
The Frankfurter Allgemeine daily said that one of Bubis' greatest achievements was to draw a clear distinction between Nazi Germany and contemporary Germany.

It said that the former Frankfurt businessman soon became an outspoken critic of attacks on foreigners and asylum seekers, and anti-Semitism during a wave of neo-Nazi violence after German unification in 1990.

"Bubis warned and admonished relentlessly at home, while for the outside world he became a convincing witness to the fact that today's Germany can not be equated with the Weimar Republic (Germany between the wars)."
Bubis reiterated his conviction that neo-Nazis and right-wing extremists do not pose a serious danger in Germany.
"Right-wing extremism and neo-Nazism are actually weaker in Germany than in its neighbouring countries, but they will always be given more attention in Germany," he told Reuters.
"But one must realise the potential is always there... There are overt and latent extremist tendencies in Germany."

Commentators recalled the time, before he became Germany's Jewish leader, when he climbed on stage with other protesters during a performance of a play by film director Rainer Werner Fassbinder in 1985 featuring a character called "the Rich Jew".
"I refused to accept that Jews and non-Jews living side by side meant that Jews could be insulted just because they were Jewish," Bubis recently told the Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily.
Born in what is now Wroclaw, Poland, Bubis lost his father, a brother and a sister in Nazi massacres. He worked in a forced-labour camp in Poland until the war ended in 1945.
Bubis, who describes himself as a "a German citizen of the Jewish faith", told Reuters that despite the fact the Nazis killed most of his family, he does not "sit on packed luggage".

"I no longer ask myself whether I should leave Germany," Bubis said. "I frequently asked myself in 1945 if it was right to stay and I ask myself now how I did it, but I don't have any doubts about that decision anymore."
When asked by Zionists in Israel why he had not left the country like other survivors, Bubis said that if all Jews left Germany, Hitler would have finally achieved his aim.
